invariant_bindings.invariant_text: Every code path that reads or writes PII MUST be annotated with a registered ProcessingRecord.activity; unregistered activities SHALL fail at startup.
Each record MUST reference a retention_ref that resolves to a bound RetentionPolicy; dangling refs CANNOT register.
legal_basis MUST be one of GDPR Article 6(1)(a-f); free-text values SHALL raise.
transfers_outside_eea entries MUST be ISO-3166 country codes; other formats are FORBIDDEN.
export_ropa() output MUST be byte-for-byte reproducible given the same registry so auditors can hash and diff releases.

attacks.hypothesis: Registering two activities whose names differ only by Unicode homoglyphs (Latin 'a' vs Cyrillic 'а') bypasses the unregistered-activity startup check because string equality passes at one site and fails at another, letting PII reads run under a shadow record.
attacks.input_fixture: registry.register(ProcessingRecord(activity='payroll', ...)); code path annotated with activity='pаyroll' (Cyrillic а). App boots; PII read succeeds with wrong record.

attacks.hypothesis: Race between RetentionPolicy unbind and ProcessingRecord.register: policy exists at resolve-time, is deleted by another thread before the record is committed. Registry ends up holding a dangling retention_ref that the invariant says cannot exist.
attacks.input_fixture: Thread A: registry.register(record with retention_ref='R1'); Thread B: policies.unbind('R1') interleaved between resolve and commit.

attacks.hypothesis: If a PII-reading code path lives inside a lazily-imported module (imported only on first HTTP request, not at startup), the startup enforcement check never sees that code path and the invariant 'unregistered activities SHALL fail at startup' is trivially bypassed. Any module loaded via importlib.import_module inside a request handler, or behind a conditional import guarded by a feature flag, is invisible to a static-annotation scanner that runs at process startup.

register() validates that retention_ref resolves to a bound RetentionPolicy at registration time, but if the RetentionPolicy store allows unbinding or deletion after registration (e.g., calling policy_store.remove('ret-90d')), the dangling-ref invariant is bypassed post-registration. The record persists in the registry with a ref that no longer resolves, violating the invariant at export or audit time without failing at registration.
attacks.input_fixture:
policy_store.bind('ret-90d', RetentionPolicy(days=90))
rec = ProcessingRecord(activity='user.read', controller='Acme', purposes=('analytics',), data_classes=('email',), recipients=(), retention_ref='ret-90d', legal_basis='6(1)(f)')
registry.register(rec)  # succeeds
policy_store.remove('ret-90d')  # now dangling
rota_bytes = registry.export_ropa()  # exports a record with dangling ref

attacks.hypothesis: legal_basis validation likely compares against an allowlist of ASCII strings like '6(1)(a)'. A Unicode homoglyph substitution — replacing Latin characters with visually identical Cyrillic or Greek codepoints — may pass a naive string equality or regex check if the validator normalizes to NFC but not NFKC, or skips unicode normalization entirely. The stored value looks correct to humans in logs/exports but is not one of the six permitted bases.
attacks.input_fixture:
# Cyrillic 'а' (U+0430) instead of Latin 'a' (U+0061)
homoglyph_basis = '6(1)(а)'  # visually: 6(1)(a)
rec = ProcessingRecord(
    activity='payment.charge', controller='Acme',
    purposes=('billing',), data_classes=('card_number',),
    recipients=(), retention_ref='ret-7y',
    legal_basis=homoglyph_basis
)
registry.register(rec)  # hypothesis: does NOT raise

attacks.hypothesis: 'UK' is the common abbreviation for the United Kingdom but is NOT a valid ISO-3166-1 alpha-2 code; the correct code is 'GB'. A validator that checks len==2 and isalpha() but does not consult the actual ISO-3166 country list will accept 'UK', 'EU', 'XX', and other plausible-looking non-codes, silently producing a compliance record that claims transfers to a code that resolves to nothing under GDPR adequacy decisions.

export_ropa() must be byte-for-byte reproducible. If the registry stores records in a plain Python set or inserts into a dict and then iterates it during serialization without an explicit sort key, record ordering will vary between Python interpreter runs (hash randomization is on by default since Python 3.3). Two audit snapshots of the same logical registry will differ in byte content and their SHA-256 hashes will diverge, breaking the auditor diff workflow.
attacks.input_fixture:
import subprocess, hashlib
# Run export in two fresh interpreter processes with same registry state
script = '''
from compliance import ProcessingRegistry, ProcessingRecord
r = ProcessingRegistry()
for i in range(20):
    r.register(ProcessingRecord(activity=f'act.{i}', controller='Acme', purposes=(f'p{i}',), data_classes=(f'd{i}',), recipients=(), retention_ref='ret-1y', legal_basis='6(1)(b)'))
print(hashlib.sha256(r.export_ropa()).hexdigest())
'''
hashes = {subprocess.check_output(['python3', '-c', script]).strip() for _ in range(5)}
print(f'Unique hashes across 5 runs: {len(hashes)}')  # hypothesis: > 1

attacks.hypothesis: If ProcessingRegistry has no internal locking, a thread calling register() concurrently with a thread calling export_ropa() may observe a partially-written registry state. Two concurrent export_ropa() calls on the same registry instance may produce different byte sequences — violating reproducibility — or a register() may corrupt the internal collection mid-iteration during export, causing a RuntimeError or silently dropping records from the output.

The dataclass accepts empty tuples for purposes and data_classes because they are typed as tuple[str, ...] with no minimum-length constraint. A ProcessingRecord with purposes=() and data_classes=() is semantically meaningless — it declares a processing activity without stating what personal data is processed or why — yet the frozen dataclass will accept it and register() will store it, producing a ROPA entry that an auditor cannot meaningfully validate.
attacks.input_fixture:
rec = ProcessingRecord(
    activity='user.profile.read',
    controller='Acme Corp',
    purposes=(),          # empty — no stated purpose
    data_classes=(),      # empty — no stated data class
    recipients=(),
    retention_ref='ret-90d',
    legal_basis='6(1)(f)'
)
registry.register(rec)  # hypothesis: succeeds without raising
ropa = registry.export_ropa()  # produces ROPA with vacuous record

attacks.hypothesis: Injecting a null byte into the activity string (e.g., 'user.read\x00.admin') may cause the annotation scanner to match 'user.read' in the registered activity (if it uses a null-terminated C string comparison under the hood or truncates at null), while the actual code path is annotated with the full string including the null byte suffix. The scanner sees a match; the audit sees the full string; the two do not refer to the same logical activity.
attacks.input_fixture:
rec_clean = ProcessingRecord(activity='user.read', controller='Acme', purposes=('analytics',), data_classes=('email',), recipients=(), retention_ref='ret-90d', legal_basis='6(1)(f)')
rec_null = ProcessingRecord(activity='user.read\x00.admin', controller='Acme', purposes=('admin_access',), data_classes=('password_hash',), recipients=(), retention_ref='ret-90d', legal_basis='6(1)(f)')
registry.register(rec_clean)
registry.register(rec_null)  # hypothesis: both register; scanner matches both against 'user.read'

attacks.hypothesis: A legal_basis value of '6(1)(a) ' (trailing space) or ' 6(1)(a)' (leading space) is not one of the six GDPR Article 6(1) bases but may slip past a validator that strips whitespace before comparison. Conversely, a validator that does NOT strip whitespace will correctly reject it — but then a developer who copy-pastes from a YAML config file with trailing newlines will be unable to register a valid record, causing false failures. Either path is a defect.

If register() does not detect duplicate activity names, a caller can register the same activity twice with different legal_basis values (e.g., first '6(1)(b)' then '6(1)(a)'). The registry holds two records for 'user.read', making the ROPA ambiguous and auditor diff non-idempotent — replaying the same registration sequence twice yields a registry with 4 records, not 2, and export_ropa() output changes with each replay, breaking reproducibility.
attacks.input_fixture:
for legal_basis in ['6(1)(a)', '6(1)(b)', '6(1)(f)']:
    rec = ProcessingRecord(
        activity='user.read',  # same activity each time
        controller='Acme',
        purposes=('analytics',), data_classes=('email',),
        recipients=(), retention_ref='ret-90d',
        legal_basis=legal_basis
    )
    registry.register(rec)

ropa1 = registry.export_ropa()
for legal_basis in ['6(1)(a)', '6(1)(b)', '6(1)(f)']:
    rec = ProcessingRecord(activity='user.read', controller='Acme', purposes=('analytics',), data_classes=('email',), recipients=(), retention_ref='ret-90d', legal_basis=legal_basis)
    registry.register(rec)
ropa2 = registry.export_ropa()
print(f'Reproducible: {ropa1 == ropa2}')  # hypothesis: False

attacks.hypothesis: ProcessingRecord is frozen=True which prevents direct attribute assignment, but object.__setattr__() or __dict__ manipulation can bypass the freeze on CPython. An attacker who obtains a reference to a registered record can mutate its legal_basis to an invalid value after registration, so the in-registry object no longer satisfies the legal_basis invariant without triggering any validation.
attacks.input_fixture:
rec = ProcessingRecord(activity='payment.charge', controller='Acme', purposes=('billing',), data_classes=('card_number',), recipients=(), retention_ref='ret-7y', legal_basis='6(1)(b)')
registry.register(rec)
# Bypass frozen=True
object.__setattr__(rec, 'legal_basis', 'free_text_anything')
print(rec.legal_basis)  # hypothesis: 'free_text_anything'
ropa = registry.export_ropa()  # exports record with invalid legal_basis

attacks.hypothesis: If export_ropa() embeds a generation timestamp (common in compliance documents), two calls to export_ropa() one second apart will differ byte-for-byte even when the registry is identical. This trivially breaks the auditor-hash-and-diff workflow described in the reproducibility invariant. The defect is silent: each export is internally self-consistent but no two exports hash the same.
attacks.input_fixture:
import time, hashlib
rec = ProcessingRecord(activity='user.read', controller='Acme', purposes=('analytics',), data_classes=('email',), recipients=(), retention_ref='ret-90d', legal_basis='6(1)(f)')
registry.register(rec)
export1 = registry.export_ropa()
time.sleep(1.1)
export2 = registry.export_ropa()
print(f'Byte-identical: {export1 == export2}')  # hypothesis: False due to embedded timestamp

attacks.hypothesis: export_ropa() builds and serializes the full registry into memory. An attacker who can call register() many times (e.g., via a public API endpoint that wraps a registry) can inflate the registry to millions of records, causing export_ropa() to allocate O(N) memory and spend O(N) CPU. A single export call on a 10M-record registry could exhaust heap and crash the compliance audit process.
